newsitem.title: FRANCE: French minister sticks to immigration bill.
newsitem.headline: French minister sticks to immigration bill.

text.p: French Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre on Tuesday defended his controversial immigration bill as a rampart against welfare scroungers as parliament prepared to give it a final reading amid a new wave of protests.
The conservative Gaullist minister accused left-wing critics of "lies, hypocrisy and manipulation" over the bill, designed to tighten controls and make it easier to expel illegal immigrants.
Opponents say the bill panders to the extreme-right National Front's anti-immigration crusade and could spread racism and xenophobia by turning all immigrants into suspects.

But Debre said in a Europe 1 radio interview: "If we want to integrate foreigners into the national community, if we want to turn back racism and xenophobia in this country, we have to fight illegal immigration."

And Prime Minister Alain Juppe charged in an article in the newspaper Le Monde that the bill's critics were playing into the hands of the National Front by blurring the distinction between legal and illegal immigration.
Using an argument often brandished by the National Front, Debre depicted recent immigrants as welfare scroungers.

He said the nature of immigration into France had changed in the last few years from "workers who wanted to integrate into the national community to claimants who want to take advantage of our welfare system and don't want to integrate".

Parliament's legal committee has removed the bill's most fiercely contested clause, which would have required French hosts to report to the police when foreign guests subject to visa requirements left their homes.

Instead, foreigners on short-term visas will be required to report their own departure to the authorities, and government prefects instead of local mayors will be responsible for issuing "accommodation certificates".

But intellectuals and artists campaigning against the legislation, who led an estimated 100,000-strong demonstration in Paris on Saturday, planned a fresh protest outside parliament on Tuesday to demand the complete withdrawal of the bill.

The opposition Socialists and Communists, largely absent from parliament when the bill was first debated in December, have submitted a welter of motions to delay or amend the bill and the National Assembly debate is expected to last three days.
Their tactics had almost no chance of success since the centre-right coalition holds four-fifths of the 577 assembly seats.
Among the bill's measures are an extension of the period for which illegal aliens may be held without trial and a provision enabling the police to raid illegal workshops.

The National Front's number two, Bruno Megret, dismissed the bill in a statement as a "political fraud", which he said showed the government was impotent in combating immigration and weak-kneed towards what he called the "human rights lobby".

The left-wing daily Liberation published a supplement on Tuesday with 55,000 signatures on petitions demanding the scrapping of the legislation. Some of the petitions also advocated civil disobedience if the bill became law.
But Debre noted opinion polls had shown a clear majority of up to 69 percent of voters support his amended bill.
The degree of public support prompted some conservative politicians to suggest President Jacques Chirac should call a referendum on immigration policy.
Debre said critics had created the impression that the bill would affect the 80 million foreigners who visit France each year whereas if would only affect some 150,000 people.
At present only one detected illegal immigrant in three was actually expelled, he said.

The foreigners concerned are mainly from Third World countries, but they also include nationals of Romania, whose President Emil Constantinescu publicly complained to Chirac last Saturday about France's restrictive visa policy.
